query: For as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys intended for magnetic refrigeration, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their magnetocaloric response and hysteresis during low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles? Earlier work focused mainly on arc-melted ingots and melt-spun microribbons, where an ordered single-phase hexagonal state undergoes a first-order magnetostructural transition that produces a large but sharp and hysteretic entropy change; these bulk forms also have limited heat-exchange rates because of their low surface-to-volume ratio. Prior searches have largely emphasized composition-dependent changes in transition temperature or response amplitude, with most studies pursuing only one optimization variable. Under the constraints of avoiding rare-earth elements, retaining mechanical stability and low cost, enabling rapid heat exchange, and limiting hysteretic losses, specify one controlled intervention that would distinguish the proposed governing explanation from alternatives, the predicted observations relative to the as-deposited baseline, the boundaries over which those predictions should hold, the prior observations that support the hypothesis, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The introduction of a small amount of a FCC-stabilizing element, such as Cu, to the non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloy will improve the magnetocaloric response and reduce the hysteresis losses by reducing the distribution of exchange energies in the system and leading to a more magnetically homogeneous alloy.

generation.boundary: The predicted outcome should hold for a range of Cu concentrations and processing conditions, but may be limited by the stability of the alloy and the effectiveness of the Cu introduction
generation.uncertainty: The exact amount and type of FCC-stabilizing element required to achieve the optimal magnetocaloric response and reduction in hysteresis losses is uncertain and requires further optimization

falsification_experiment.design: Measure the magnetocaloric response and hysteresis losses of the alloy with and without the introduction of Cu, and compare the results to the predicted outcome
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the introduction of Cu does not lead to an improvement in the magnetocaloric response and a reduction in the hysteresis losses, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: Delving deeper, unfortunately, RCP tends to overestimate the merits of the materials which have a large temperature range of magnetocaloric effect (δTFWHM) but small entropy changes [,] in no small part because materials with same relative cooling power can behave differently in a magnetic cooling simulation []. Moreover, one of the last printed books about magnetic cooling ignores this figure of merit []. In order to be of use in magnetic refrigeration applications the chosen materials have to show a large magnetocaloric effect—a large magnetic entropy change. Besides this, there is a list of requirements related with heat transfer, heat capacity, heat conductivity, chemical and mechanical stability, hysteresis losses, eddy currents losses, etc. Therefore, magnetic measurements can be a trusted guide in deciding if a material deserves the effort of complete characterization. Some compounds of the type A1−xBxMnO3 can be considered to be of interest for magnetic refrigeration because some of these compounds show −ΔSm values (−ΔSm ≈ 4–6 J·kg−1·K−1 for ΔH = 5 T) comparable to intermetallic alloys []. This is the case of our investigated compounds.

The unpredictability of geopolitical tensions and resulting supply chain and pricing instabilities make it imperative to explore rare earth free magnetic materials. As such, we have investigated fully transition metal based “high entropy alloys” in the context of the magnetocaloric effect. We find the NiFeCoCrPdx family exhibits a second order magnetic phase transition whose critical temperature is tunable from 100 K to well above room temperature. The system notably displays changes in the functionality of the magnetic entropy change depending on x, which leads to nearly 40% enhancement of the refrigerant capacity. A detailed statistical analysis of the universal scaling behavior provides direct evidence that heat treatment and Pd additions reduce the distribution of exchange energies in the system, leading to a more magnetically homogeneous alloy. The general implications of this work are that the parent NiFeCoCr compound can be tuned dramatically with FCC metal additives. Our results show there is a major impact on magnetic properties of this novel class of materials with FCC metal additions, even at small concentrations. The NiFeCoCrPdx displays a second order magnetic phase transition that is tunable from room temperature down to around 100 K as x decreases from 11.11% down to 0.00%. While the magnetic entropy change for the transition only increases slightly with Pd, the refrigerant capacity improves by nearly 40%. The latter observation is related to increasingly superlinear behavior of the field dependence of the refrigerant capacity with Pd content. This increase in field dependence may be attributed to increased magnetic homogeneity within the alloy as a result of both Pd additions and annealing, which appear to reduce the distribution of exchange energies in the system. The initially wide distribution of exchange energies is at least the result of structural defects, and possibly due to an unidentified minority phase (as has been observed in other HEAs).
